If you have a solid self assessment of what you know, you can consider when information is supported by what you know. For the parts that aren't, you consider how critical they are, and identify the area that needs a deeper dive, where you either link it back to other areas you have confidence in your own knowledge or work to expand your own knowledge (using other resources). Then cross check knowledge. The cheap way you can do easily is to cross check between AIs/harnesses, because hallucinations happen randomly, so two different models in two different harnesses having the same hallucination is extremely rare. The more expensive option, which should be used when the information really matters, is building your own knowledge. Have the AI help guide you to resources, but not be the resource. While using non-AI resources, check you knowledge against them and the AI. Test yourself with classical resources where it really matters.

Part of it is using good judgment. Is the AI's claim reasonable if it came from another person? If some random person gave you a 2 page paper proving P=NP, would you even spend time to look at it, or would you simply toss it without caring to understand what error they made. Much like how scientists (and even the patent office) simply refuse to entertain any perpetual motion machines. Maybe if an expert in the field proposed it, and even that would depend upon how ("Hey, I found a source of free energy!" vs "Hey, I'm working through these equations and the energy term isn't balancing, can you help me find what energy source I'm missing?").

This does pose a problem. Those who are the best at understanding the limits of their knowledge and at teaching themselves need the AI's help the least but are in the position to be able to use AI with the best chance of not being misled. Those who lack these skills and would benefit the most from a personal educator, thus receving the biggest benefit in theory, are the ones most likely to fall victim to the errors made by the AI.

Same here. There is an introspective comment below by khazhoux asking the question from the opposite experience. Why do developers end up on different sides of this coin?

LLM capability is obviously important variable. But those with bad experiences report using top tier models, so that isn't it. Likewise, level of experience can be ruled out. Each side of the coin have experienced developers reporting.

A lot of the other variables are not reported but I can go from my own experience.

Greenfield vs brownfield? The first is indeed usually easier but I get great results updating large code bases with decades of development. And I suspect developing greenfield with LLM is easier as the code is better written from the start.

Rarity of the subject matter? In principle, yet another XYZ app or web page is well represented in the training data so the LLM should have an easy go at making similar. In the past with low-end LLMs, this was noticeable. Working in relatively obscure programming languages produced just garbage. But, that was prior to the inflection point. And today I get good results working on relatively arcane scientific/mathematical algorithm as I do when I ask the LLM to barf out some web app.

Different levels of testing and validation and expectation? Even best LLMs make mistakes. The better LLMs make fewer and expose fewer still to the human as they create internal tests. Maybe people have different expectations and those with bad experience expect perfection from a single prompt? Perhaps, but any experienced developer knows bugs are a part of software development.

What else?

Whatever the answer, it's not a simple one and it may be a confluence of many smaller things. Maybe different developers have a multi-variant function in their brain that pops out a different quality-of-software score and also a different threshold that divides good from bad and all we see in their reports is that binary conclusion.

I think people underestimate where most of the work goes in rebuilding a platform like Word or Excel. Getting the UI and common cases working is the easy part. The bulk of the effort is dealing with edge cases and exceptions.

The file format docs don't tell you everything about how Excel or Word actually behaves. And a collection of public files will only get you so far. A lot of the weird stuff shows up in proprietary files that customers have been building and modifying for years.

You get a file from one customer, find a case you've never seen, figure out what Office does, implement it, and make sure you haven't broken something else. Then the next customer sends you another one, and so on.

That cycle takes years. Reading and writing DOCX or XLSX is great, but getting close to full compatibility is a much bigger job.
